summary: Defines a response set describing assertions a reputation provider can make about email identifiers, for generating reputons. It is part of a small family of reputation documents.

plainLanguage.summary: The kinds of facts you can learn about an email sender.

questions: what is the email-id reputation application
what assertions can an email reputation service make
subtitle: The vocabulary a reputation service uses to say whether an email sender, domain or address is trouble.

tldr.problem: A mail system that asks a reputation service about a sender needs an agreed set of things the service can say, and a way to say which part of the message the answer is about.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7073 defines the 'email-id' reputation application with five assertions (abusive, fraud, invalid-recipients, malware, spam) and an optional 'identity' extension that names where the identifier came from, such as a DKIM signing domain or the client IP address.
tldr.outcome: It registers 'email-id' with IANA so reputation clients and providers can interoperate. All of its assertions are negative; the RFC expects positive ones to be added later.

today: RFC 7073 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7070 and RFC 7071.

sections.title: Where This Fits
sections.content:
RFC 7073 specifies a response set for describing the reputation of an email identifier. A response set, as defined in RFC 7070, holds the assertions a reputation service provider can make, plus metadata that can go in a reply beyond the base set.

An atomic reputation response is a reputon, defined in RFC 7071. That document also defines a media type to carry a reputon and creates a registry of reputation applications and their parameters. RFC 7073 adds one entry to that registry.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a way to pass reputation notes around. This document just says what the notes about email can say.

sections.title: The Five Assertions
sections.content:
The email-id reputation application recognizes five assertions about a subject identifier:

  • abusive: associated with sending or handling email that is personally abusive, threatening or harassing.
  • fraud: associated with fraudulent email such as phishing.
  • invalid-recipients: associated with delivery attempts to nonexistent recipients.
  • malware: associated with sending or handling malware via email.
  • spam: associated with unwanted bulk email.

For every assertion the rating scale is linear. A value of 0.0 means there is no data to support the assertion, 1.0 means all accumulated data support it, and a score of x is twice as strong as x/2.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note can say one of five things, like 'sends scams' or 'sends junk'. A number from 0 to 1 says how sure the club is, where 1 means very sure.

sections.title: The Identity and Sources Extensions
sections.content:
The application recognizes two OPTIONAL extensions to the basic response set. email-id-identity is a token that says where the subject identifier was found in the message. It MUST be one of:

  • dkim: the signing domain (the d= tag) of a valid DKIM signature.
  • ipv4 or ipv6: the address of the client.
  • rfc5321.helo: the HELO value used by the client.
  • rfc5321.mailfrom: the MailFrom value in the envelope.
  • rfc5322.from: the From field of the message.
  • spf: the domain of the identifier (MailFrom or HELO) verified by SPF.

The second extension, sources, is a token counting how many sources of data contributed to the reputation. It differs from sample-size, which is the total number of reports across all sources. A reply with neither extension makes a non-specific statement about how the reputation was developed, and a client can use or ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: A note can also say where the name came from, such as the return address on the envelope or a signature that was checked. It can also say how many different helpers gave information.

sections.title: Strong and Weak Identifiers
sections.content:
One message can carry several identifiers. The MailFrom and the From header can show different addresses, and the HELO value will differ again, so a client may need to query more than one identifier.

The identity token tells the client the context of each one. Several values are taken verbatim from the message and have not been validated, while a domain in a valid DKIM signature has more reliable meaning. Reputation for unauthenticated identifiers has substantially reduced value, but can be useful in combination. One weak identifier with a high spam rating may not deserve notice, while several of them could be grounds for suspicion.

For weaker identifiers, a client queries each with the same assertion and collates the results. For stronger identifiers, a decision can typically rest on a few or even one of them. A query can also carry the OPTIONAL identity parameter to say which identity it is asking about.
sections.plainLanguage: A name written on an envelope could be faked, but a checked signature is harder to fake. So you trust the checked ones more and look for patterns among the unchecked ones.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content:
The only IANA action is registering the email-id reputation application under RFC 7071. Its short description is that it evaluates DNS domain names or IP addresses found in email identifiers, and its status is current.

The registration lists one application-specific query parameter, identity, the five assertions, and one response set extension, identity. The subject is a string appropriate to the identifier of interest.
sections.plainLanguage: The document signs 'email-id' into the official list of reputation topics so everyone uses the same name.

sections.title: Security and the Negative Slant
sections.content:
The RFC says it is primarily an IANA action and describes no protocol elements that introduce new security concerns. It points to the documents it references for email security, and to a work-in-progress draft on operational considerations for reputation services.

Appendix A notes that current theories suggest it may have more impact to build positive reputations and give preferential treatment to sources that earn them. Yet every assertion in this document is negative. The RFC records current use and expects later registrations to focus on positive assertions.
sections.plainLanguage: This document does not add new ways to break things. It only lists bad-news words, and the authors expect good-news words to be added later.
